newsitem.title: USA: Utah's Sundance festival gets under way.
newsitem.headline: Utah's Sundance festival gets under way.

text.p: The Sundance Film Festival has become the Mecca of independent films, but while many are called few are chosen.

Of 800 entries submitted for showing at this year's 10-day festival starting on Thursday, 127 feature films and 56 short entries have been selected. "There are so many films being produced right now, the standards of getting a work into the theatrical realm is such a high hurdle, that the work has to be good," festival director Geoffrey Gilmore told Reuters.
The chosen few will be viewed at 13 theatre in this ski town and and four other places including the Sundance Resort, home of festival founder and actor-director Robert Redford.

To open the festival, 17 films will be shown including "Brassed Off," a story of a working class town in Britain, and "SubUrbia," a Generation X film about disaffected youth written by Eric Bogosian, based on his play of the same name.
Also premiering is the docu-drama "Prefontaine" about distance runner Stefe Prefontaine, written and directed by "Hoop Dreams" filmmaker Steve James.

In the past independent films often meant obscure entries and unknown actors, but those days are over. At this year's festival, director David Lynch will present the world premier of "Lost Highway" with Bill Pullman and Patricia Arquette while Peter Fonda will star in Victor Nunez's "Ulee's Gold."
The festival will also feature an opening day tribute to actor Tim Robbins and a retrospective of the films of German director R.W. Fassbinder.
More than 9,000 people braved a major snowstorm last year to attend Sundance events.

Besides providing filmmakers a chance to show off their works, the festival offers them an opportunity to rub shoulders with movie industry leaders. Park City, a posh ski resort that was once a silver mining town, has become Hollywood East, swarming with film industry executives, producers, writers and directors in search of their next project.
"Big Night," "The Spitfire Grill" and "Lone Star" picked up distribution contracts after their showings last year.
For director Neil LaBute, whose feature film "In the Company of Men" is one of 18 films in the dramatic competition, just getting his work shown is reward enough.
"Honestly, this is what we were shooting for; getting it into the festival," he said by telephone from his Fort Wayne, Indiana home. "Getting a film in the festival is ... such a long shot."

His film is a dark comedy about male ego in which two businessmen, bored with their careers, decide to toy with the emotions of a young woman they both date at the same time. What starts out as a prank becomes a tale of deceit, manipulation, betrayal and hurt.

"Sundance, under Redford, has become something unique," LaBute said. "It can handle having major stars and films of international import and still maintain its integrity in terms of the independent market."
